course.title: Ecology
course.description: Ecology is the study of how organisms interact with one another and with their physical surroundings, from a single population up to the whole biosphere. This course walks through the levels of organization, population and community dynamics, energy flow, nutrient cycles, biodiversity, and the growing human footprint on natural systems. The structure and framing draw on the Ecology overview from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0), with all prose written fresh.

questions.prompt: Ecology is best described as the study of...
options: interactions among organisms and their environment
the internal anatomy of a single cell
questions.explanation: Ecology examines how living things relate to each other and to their physical surroundings - see 'What ecology studies'.

questions.prompt: Ordered from smallest to largest, the levels of ecological organization are...
questions.explanation: Each level nests inside the next: organism, population, community, ecosystem, biosphere.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an abiotic factor?
questions.explanation: Abiotic means nonliving; temperature is a physical property of the environment.

questions.prompt: Carrying capacity refers to...
options: the fastest a population could ever grow
the maximum population an environment can sustain over time
the total mass of all producers
the number of species in a community
questions.explanation: It is the long-term ceiling an environment can support - see 'Population ecology'.

questions.prompt: A relationship in which both species benefit is called...
questions.explanation: Mutualism is the plus-plus case where both partners gain.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of energy is passed from one trophic level to the next?
questions.explanation: The ten percent rule: most energy is lost as heat at each step.

questions.prompt: The process by which certain bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms usable by plants is...
questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation turns inert atmospheric nitrogen into nitrates plants can absorb.

questions.prompt: Which human activity is generally considered the leading cause of biodiversity loss?
questions.explanation: Clearing habitat for farming, logging, and cities is the largest single driver.

lessons.title: What ecology studies and the levels of organization
lessons.grammar_note: A population is one species in one place; a community is many species together. Keep those two straight and the rest of ecology lines up.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Say in plain words what ecology studies, separate it from neighboring sciences like physiology and evolution, and sort any living example into the correct level of organization. By the end you should be able to read a statement such as 'wolves control deer numbers in a valley' and name which levels it touches. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, list the five levels of organization from smallest to largest before you read on, then check yourself as you go. This lesson is the map for the whole course, so take time to make the vocabulary feel natural rather than memorized.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Ecology is the scientific study of the relationships between living organisms, including humans, and their physical environment. It asks where organisms live, how abundant they are, and why. Ecologists organize nature into nested levels. An organism is a single living individual. A population is all the individuals of one species in one area. A community is all the interacting populations of different species in that area. An ecosystem adds the nonliving environment, linking the community to the flow of energy and matter. The biosphere is the sum of all ecosystems, the global zone where life exists. Each level shows properties the smaller one lacks: a population has a growth rate, a community has a food web, an ecosystem has nutrient cycling. Ecology overlaps with but differs from physiology, which studies how one body works, and from evolution, which studies change across generations.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Consider a mountain meadow. One marmot is an organism. All the marmots in the meadow form a population, which you might count to estimate density. The marmots, the grasses they eat, the eagles that hunt them, and the soil microbes together make a community, studied through their interactions. Add sunlight, rainfall, rock, and the movement of nutrients and you have an ecosystem, where energy enters through plants and matter returns through decomposers. Zoom out to every meadow, forest, ocean, and desert on Earth and you reach the biosphere. Ecologists pick the level that matches the question. To ask why marmot numbers rose this year, work at the population level. To ask how a drought reshuffled who eats whom, work at the community level. To track where carbon goes, work at the ecosystem level. Matching the question to the right level keeps an investigation focused and testable.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the level: all the oak trees in one forest. 2) Name the level: oak trees plus squirrels plus fungi plus the soil and climate of that forest. 3) Which level has a food web as a property? 4) Is 'how a frog's heart pumps blood' an ecology question? 5) Which level is the largest? Answers: 1) a population, one species in one area. 2) an ecosystem, because it adds the nonliving surroundings. 3) the community level, where multiple species interact. 4) no, that is physiology, the workings of one organism. 5) the biosphere, all ecosystems combined across the whole planet.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using 'population' and 'community' as if they mean the same thing; a population is one species, a community is many species together. Mistake: calling any group of living things an ecosystem; an ecosystem must also include the nonliving environment and the exchange of energy and matter. Exit: (a) What is the difference between a community and an ecosystem? (b) Order these from small to large: community, organism, biosphere, population, ecosystem. Answers: a community is the living species together, while an ecosystem adds the nonliving surroundings and the flow of energy and nutrients; organism, population, community, ecosystem, biosphere.

lessons.title: Abiotic factors and biomes
lessons.grammar_note: Abiotic means nonliving, biotic means living. If you can ask whether it was ever alive, you are testing whether a factor is biotic.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Identify the main abiotic factors that shape where life can live, explain how temperature and precipitation together define the world's biomes, and predict the dominant vegetation of a region from its climate. Warm-up: before reading, guess which two abiotic factors matter most for telling a desert apart from a rainforest, then see whether the lesson confirms your hunch. Keep a real place you know in mind and try to classify its biome as you work through the ideas below.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Abiotic factors are the nonliving physical and chemical parts of the environment: temperature, light, water, wind, soil, salinity, and the supply of mineral nutrients. They set the limits within which organisms can survive and reproduce. Each species tolerates a range for every factor, and where ranges overlap favorably the species can persist. Two abiotic factors, average temperature and annual precipitation, do most of the work in sorting land into biomes, which are large regions sharing a characteristic climate and community type. Tropical rainforests are warm and wet; deserts are dry; tundra is cold with a short growing season; temperate grasslands get moderate, seasonal rain. Aquatic systems are divided instead by salinity, depth, and flow into freshwater and marine zones. Because climate drives vegetation and vegetation shapes animal life, knowing a region's temperature and rainfall predicts a great deal about what lives there.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Picture moving from the equator toward a pole. Near the equator, steady warmth and heavy rain support tropical rainforest, the most productive and species-rich land biome. Move into drier belts and you reach savanna and then desert, where water, not warmth, is the limiting abiotic factor. In the mid-latitudes, temperate forests and grasslands follow the rhythm of seasonal temperature and moderate rain. Far north lies the taiga of conifers, and beyond it the treeless tundra, where cold and a frozen subsoil cap plant growth. Elevation repeats this sequence in miniature: climbing a tall mountain carries you from warm forest at the base to cold, tundra-like slopes near the summit, because temperature falls with altitude. Ecologists summarize these patterns with climate diagrams that plot a site's monthly temperature and rainfall, letting them match an unfamiliar place to its likely biome and its expected community of species.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Is soil pH an abiotic or biotic factor? 2) Which two abiotic factors most strongly define land biomes? 3) What limits plant growth in the tundra? 4) Why does climbing a mountain resemble traveling toward a pole? 5) What mainly distinguishes a desert from a rainforest? Answers: 1) abiotic, it is a chemical property of the nonliving soil. 2) temperature and precipitation. 3) cold temperatures and a short growing season over frozen subsoil. 4) temperature drops with altitude just as it drops with latitude, so the vegetation zones stack up in a similar order. 5) mainly the amount of precipitation, with deserts being very dry.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating sunlight or soil as biotic because living things use them; a factor is biotic only if it is or once was alive. Mistake: thinking a biome is a single place rather than a climate-defined type that recurs on different continents. Exit: (a) Give three abiotic factors. (b) A warm, wet region near the equator most likely holds which biome? Answers: any three of temperature, light, water, wind, soil, salinity, or mineral nutrients; tropical rainforest, the warm and wet biome.

lessons.title: Population ecology: growth, limits, and carrying capacity
lessons.grammar_note: Exponential growth bends upward without limit; logistic growth levels off at the carrying capacity. Picture a J-curve versus an S-curve.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how populations change in size, tell exponential growth from logistic growth, explain carrying capacity, and classify limiting factors as density-dependent or density-independent. Warm-up: if a pond starts with 2 lily pads and the number doubles every day, is that growth exponential or logistic, and what will eventually slow it? Hold that example in mind; by the end of the lesson you should be able to explain exactly why the pond cannot keep doubling forever.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Population ecology studies the size, density, and structure of populations and the forces that make them rise or fall. Four processes change a population: births and immigration add individuals, deaths and emigration remove them. When resources are unlimited, a population grows exponentially, producing a steep J-shaped curve because each generation is larger than the last. Real environments are not unlimited. As a population grows, food, space, and other resources run short, slowing growth until the population levels off near its carrying capacity, the maximum number the environment can support over the long run. Plotting this gives an S-shaped, or logistic, curve. Limiting factors are what hold a population in check. Density-dependent factors, such as competition, disease, and predation, bite harder as the population becomes crowded. Density-independent factors, such as floods, fire, and cold snaps, strike regardless of how many individuals are present.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Bacteria dropped into fresh nutrient broth grow almost exponentially at first, doubling again and again, until waste and scarce food slow them to a logistic plateau. A deer herd on an island with plentiful grass may overshoot its carrying capacity, then crash as starvation and disease, both density-dependent, cut numbers back toward the sustainable level. Ecologists estimate population size with sampling rather than counting every individual. Mark-and-recapture is a classic approach: capture and tag a batch of animals, release them, then later capture a second batch and use the fraction tagged to estimate the total. Quadrats, fixed sample squares, work for counting plants or slow movers. Life tables track survival and reproduction by age, revealing whether a population is growing, stable, or shrinking. These tools turn a vague sense of abundance into numbers that managers can act on, for example when setting fishing limits or planning a species recovery program.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the shape of an exponential growth curve. 2) What does carrying capacity mean? 3) Classify predation: density-dependent or density-independent? 4) Classify a sudden frost: density-dependent or independent? 5) Which sampling method tags animals, releases them, and recaptures later? Answers: 1) a J-shaped curve. 2) the maximum population an environment can support over the long term. 3) density-dependent, since crowding raises each individual's chance of being eaten. 4) density-independent, a frost kills a similar fraction regardless of crowding. 5) mark-and-recapture.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming populations grow exponentially forever; limited resources force most toward a logistic plateau. Mistake: calling every limiting factor density-dependent; weather and natural disasters usually act independently of density. Exit: (a) What curve shape describes logistic growth? (b) Give one density-dependent and one density-independent limiting factor. Answers: an S-shaped curve that levels off at the carrying capacity; density-dependent such as competition, disease, or predation, and density-independent such as flood, fire, or a cold snap.

questions.prompt: A community differs from a population because a community...
questions.explanation: A population is one species; a community is many interacting species in one area.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an abiotic factor?
questions.explanation: Rainfall is a nonliving physical factor; the others are living.

questions.prompt: The two abiotic factors that most strongly define land biomes are...
questions.explanation: Average temperature and annual precipitation sort land into its major biomes.

questions.prompt: Unlimited resources would produce which growth pattern?
questions.explanation: With no limits each generation is larger, giving a J-shaped exponential curve.

questions.prompt: A population that overshoots its carrying capacity will most likely...
questions.explanation: Density-dependent factors like starvation push an overshooting population back down.

questions.prompt: Disease spreading faster in a crowded population is an example of a...
questions.explanation: Its effect grows with crowding, which is the signature of a density-dependent factor.

lessons.title: Species interactions, community ecology, and succession
lessons.grammar_note: For symbiosis, think plus-plus for mutualism, plus-minus for predation and parasitism, and plus-zero for commensalism. The signs tell you who gains and who loses.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name and recognize the main ways species interact, explain how those interactions shape a community, and describe how a community rebuilds itself through ecological succession. Warm-up: a bee drinks nectar and carries pollen between flowers; who benefits in that relationship, and does anyone lose? Keep that question in view as you read, because sorting out who gains and who loses is the key skill this lesson builds, from a single pair of species up to a whole changing community.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Community ecology studies how populations of different species interact and how those interactions assemble a community. Competition occurs when two species need the same limited resource; it tends to push them to use the resource differently, a pattern called resource partitioning. Predation is one organism eating another, which can control prey numbers and drive defenses such as camouflage. Symbiosis covers close, long-term relationships: in mutualism both partners gain, in commensalism one gains while the other is unaffected, and in parasitism one gains while the other is harmed. A keystone species has an effect on its community far larger than its abundance would suggest; remove it and the community can collapse or reorganize. Over time communities change through succession. Primary succession starts on bare rock or new ground with no soil, while secondary succession follows a disturbance, such as a fire, that leaves soil behind. Pioneer species arrive first and prepare the way for later, longer-lived ones.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: On a rocky shore, removing a predatory starfish, a keystone species, lets mussels crowd out everything else and sharply lowers diversity, showing how one interaction can hold a whole community together. Competition appears when two warbler species feed in the same tree but partition it, one high in the canopy and one lower down, so both persist. Mutualism is everywhere: bees pollinate flowers while gaining nectar, and gut microbes help animals digest food. Succession is visible after a volcanic eruption lays down bare rock, where lichens and mosses, the pioneers, break rock into thin soil that grasses, then shrubs, then trees can colonize in turn. After a forest fire, secondary succession runs faster because soil and seeds survive. Ecologists track these changes with permanent plots revisited over years, recording which species appear, persist, or vanish, and they run removal experiments to test which interactions actually structure the community.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Both species benefit: which interaction? 2) One benefits and the other is harmed in a close, long-term bond: which interaction? 3) What is a keystone species? 4) Which succession begins on bare rock with no soil? 5) What are the first colonizers in succession called? Answers: 1) mutualism. 2) parasitism. 3) a species whose impact on its community is far larger than its numbers suggest. 4) primary succession. 5) pioneer species, such as lichens and mosses.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing commensalism (plus-zero) with mutualism (plus-plus); in commensalism only one partner gains while the other is unaffected. Mistake: assuming succession always starts from bare rock; secondary succession begins after a disturbance that leaves the soil intact. Exit: (a) Give the sign pattern for predation. (b) What is the main difference between primary and secondary succession? Answers: one species gains and the other loses, so plus-minus; primary succession starts where there is no soil, while secondary succession starts on existing soil after a disturbance.

lessons.title: Energy flow, trophic levels, food webs, and nutrient cycles
lessons.grammar_note: Energy flows one way and is lost as heat at each step; matter cycles and is reused. The slogan to remember is: energy flows, matter cycles.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Trace energy from the sun through trophic levels, explain why food chains are short, read a food web, and describe how carbon, nitrogen, and water cycle through an ecosystem. Warm-up: if producers capture 10,000 units of energy, roughly how much reaches a secondary consumer two steps up? Make a guess now, then check it against the worked example. This lesson ties together the single most important contrast in ecology: energy is spent, but matter is recycled again and again.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Energy enters most ecosystems as sunlight, which producers, mainly plants and algae, capture through photosynthesis and store as chemical energy. That energy passes to consumers when they feed. Each feeding step is a trophic level: producers, then primary consumers that are herbivores, then secondary and tertiary consumers that are carnivores, with decomposers breaking down dead matter at every level. Energy transfer is inefficient; only about ten percent moves from one level to the next, the rest lost as heat and in life processes. This ten percent rule is why food chains rarely exceed four or five links and why top predators are few. A food web links many chains into a realistic picture of who eats whom. Matter behaves differently. Instead of leaving as heat, chemical elements cycle through biogeochemical cycles: carbon moves between air, organisms, and soil; bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen into usable forms; and water moves through evaporation, condensation, and precipitation.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Start with grass capturing 10,000 units of energy. Grasshoppers eating it retain roughly 1,000; the shrews eating grasshoppers retain about 100; a hawk eating shrews gets about 10. Drawing this as an energy pyramid makes the losses obvious and explains why large predators need big ranges. A food web for a pond might show algae feeding insects and tadpoles, which feed fish, which feed herons, with bacteria decomposing everyone, so a change in one species ripples outward. For matter, follow a carbon atom: a plant pulls carbon dioxide from the air into sugar, an animal eats the plant and breathes some carbon back out as carbon dioxide, and decomposers return the rest to soil and air. Nitrogen fixation by soil and root bacteria converts inert atmospheric nitrogen into nitrates that plants absorb, later released again by decomposition. Ecologists measure these flows by tracking tagged isotopes and monitoring gas exchange over a study plot.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Where does energy enter most ecosystems? 2) Roughly what percentage of energy passes to the next trophic level? 3) Why are food chains short? 4) Which cycle relies on bacteria to convert an atmospheric gas into a usable form? 5) Does matter flow one way or cycle? Answers: 1) as sunlight captured by producers through photosynthesis. 2) about ten percent. 3) because so much energy is lost at each step that little remains to support many levels. 4) the nitrogen cycle, through nitrogen fixation. 5) matter cycles and is reused, unlike energy, which flows one way and leaves as heat.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: saying energy cycles the way matter does; energy flows one way and departs as heat, while matter is recycled. Mistake: thinking decomposers sit only at the top of a food chain; they act at every level, returning nutrients to the soil. Exit: (a) State the ten percent rule in one sentence. (b) Name the three biogeochemical cycles covered here. Answers: roughly ten percent of the energy at one trophic level is passed to the next, the rest lost mainly as heat; the carbon cycle, the nitrogen cycle, and the water cycle.

items.translation: a community of organisms together with the nonliving environment, linked by energy flow and nutrient cycling
items.example: A pond ecosystem includes the fish, the algae, the water, and the sunlight that powers it.

items.translation: the maximum population size an environment can support over the long term
items.example: When deer numbers passed the carrying capacity, starvation pushed the herd back down.

items.translation: a feeding position in a food chain, such as producer, herbivore, or carnivore
items.example: Energy drops by about ninety percent as it moves up each trophic level.

items.translation: a symbiotic relationship in which both species benefit
items.example: The bee and the flower share a mutualism: food for the bee, pollination for the plant.

items.translation: a species whose effect on its community is far larger than its abundance alone would suggest
items.example: The sea star is a keystone species whose removal let mussels overrun the shore.

items.translation: the gradual, orderly change in the species of a community over time
items.example: After the fire, succession moved the clearing from grasses to shrubs to young trees.

items.translation: the conversion of atmospheric nitrogen into forms plants can absorb, carried out by certain bacteria
items.example: Clover hosts root bacteria that perform nitrogen fixation, enriching the soil.

items.translation: the variety of life in an area, counted across genes, species, and ecosystems
items.example: Clearing the rainforest sharply lowers the region's biodiversity.

lessons.title: Biodiversity, conservation, human impacts, and field methods
lessons.grammar_note: Biodiversity spans three scales: genes within a species, species within a community, and ecosystems within a region. A threat can strike at any of the three.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define biodiversity and say why it matters, list the major human pressures on ecosystems, outline conservation responses, and describe the core field and research methods ecologists use to gather evidence. Warm-up: name one reason a forest with many species might withstand a drought better than a single-species plantation. This final reading pulls the course together, because protecting nature depends on measuring it well, and the methods below are how ecologists turn observation into reliable evidence.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Biodiversity is the variety of life measured across three scales: genetic diversity within a species, species diversity within a community, and ecosystem diversity across a region. It underpins services people depend on, such as pollination, clean water, fertile soil, and climate regulation, and it tends to make ecosystems more stable and resilient. Human activity now drives biodiversity loss far faster than natural background rates. The leading pressure is habitat loss from farming, logging, and urban sprawl. Invasive species, moved by trade and travel, outcompete or prey on natives that never evolved defenses against them. Pollution, including nutrient runoff, plastics, and toxic chemicals, degrades air, water, and soil. Overharvesting removes species faster than they can recover. Climate change shifts the temperature and rainfall patterns that define habitats, forcing species to move, adapt, or die. Conservation responds with protected areas, habitat restoration, laws that limit harvest and trade, captive breeding, and corridors that reconnect fragmented habitat.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Ecology rests on careful fieldwork. To estimate how many animals live in an area, researchers use mark-and-recapture, tagging a sample and later checking what fraction of a new sample carries tags. To survey plants, they lay down quadrats, fixed sample squares, and count what grows inside, or run transects, lines along which they record every species crossed. Remote cameras and acoustic recorders log shy or nocturnal animals without disturbing them, and satellite imagery tracks habitat change across whole landscapes. Controlled field experiments, such as fencing off plots to exclude grazers, test cause and effect rather than mere correlation. Long-term monitoring plots revisited for decades reveal slow trends a single visit would miss. On the conservation side, the recovery of species pulled back from the brink, achieved by protecting habitat, curbing hunting, and breeding animals for release, shows these methods guiding real action. Each tool trades off cost, precision, and disturbance, so ecologists match the method to the question and the species.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the three scales of biodiversity. 2) What is the leading cause of biodiversity loss? 3) Why can an invasive species spread so easily? 4) Which field method uses fixed sample squares to count plants? 5) Name one conservation response to habitat fragmentation. Answers: 1) genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity. 2) habitat loss from farming, logging, and urban expansion. 3) native species often lack evolved defenses against it, so it outcompetes or preys on them freely. 4) quadrat sampling. 5) wildlife corridors that reconnect separated patches of habitat.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: equating biodiversity only with the number of species, ignoring genetic and ecosystem diversity. Mistake: assuming correlation from a single survey proves cause; controlled, repeated fieldwork is what tests cause and effect. Exit: (a) List three human pressures on ecosystems. (b) Why is long-term monitoring valuable? Answers: any three of habitat loss, invasive species, pollution, overharvesting, or climate change; it reveals slow trends and rare events that a one-time survey would miss.

questions.prompt: A relationship in which one species benefits and the other is harmed over a close, long-term association is...
questions.explanation: Parasitism is the plus-minus symbiosis where one partner gains at the other's expense.

questions.prompt: Succession that begins on bare rock with no soil is called...
questions.explanation: Primary succession starts where no soil exists, as after a glacier or lava flow.

questions.prompt: About how much of the energy at one trophic level reaches the next?
questions.explanation: The ten percent rule; most energy is lost as heat and in life processes.

questions.prompt: Bacteria that convert atmospheric nitrogen into plant-usable forms carry out...
questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation turns inert atmospheric nitrogen into nitrates plants can absorb.

questions.prompt: The single largest cause of global biodiversity loss is...
questions.explanation: Clearing and fragmenting habitat for human use outranks the other drivers.

questions.prompt: Laying fixed sample squares to count plants in an area is called...
questions.explanation: Quadrats are the standard fixed-square method for surveying vegetation.
